Neonatal Caribbean gambusia emerge at a total length of approximately 1.061 centimeters [Lb = approximately 1.061 centimeters], a remarkably diminutive size for a poeciliid. This initial length is consistent among both sexes at the moment of parturition, reflecting the limited capacity of the maternal brood pouch during gestation. In laboratory-reared cohorts maintained at a constant water temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the gestation period from fertilization to eclosion lasts exactly 28 days [ab = exactly 28 days], a duration that aligns well with the incubation times documented for other Gambusia species kept under similar thermal regimes. The wet weight of these newborn individuals averages 0.0115 grams [Wwb = 0.0115 grams], a value derived from the species-specific length–weight power relationship. This modest birth mass underscores the substantial energetic bottleneck faced by the yolk-sac larva immediately after chorion rupture, as it must quickly develop the mouth gape and retinal differentiation necessary to initiate exogenous feeding before its limited yolk reserves are entirely exhausted.

A pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size characterizes Gambusia puncticulata, with females attaining a significantly larger final length than males. The maximum total length recorded for adult females reaches 4.600 centimeters [Li = 4.600 centimeters], whereas the largest males rarely exceed 2.700 centimeters [Li = 2.700 centimeters]. This disparity is also reflected in the asymptotic wet weights; a fully grown female typically weighs 1.12 grams [Wwi = 1.12 grams], while the ultimate wet weight of a male is only 0.21 grams [Wwi = 0.21 grams]. Such a stark difference between the sexes is a common feature in the Poeciliidae, often interpreted as a consequence of fecundity selection acting more strongly on females, whose body cavity volume directly constrains litter size. These weight estimates were computed using the same allometric equation that successfully predicts mass from length in newborn individuals, ensuring consistency across ontogenetic stages.

Under a stable thermal environment of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the timing of key developmental milestones follows a predictable schedule. For females, the time since birth at puberty is 5 weeks since birth [tp = 5 weeks since birth], which corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and the initial maturation of ovarian follicles at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. Males, in contrast, reach puberty sooner, achieving sexual maturity at 4 weeks after parturition [tp = 4 weeks after parturition], a difference likely driven by the lower energetic demands of testicular development relative to the substantial resource investment required for oocyte production at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. In terms of body size, females reach this maturational milestone at a total length of 2.720 centimeters [Lp = 2.720 centimeters], whereas males mature at a smaller total length of 2.151 centimeters [Lp = 2.151 centimeters]. This accelerated male maturation is ecologically advantageous, ensuring that a pool of reproductively viable males is available to fertilize the first mature oocytes of slightly older females. It is important to note that these ages at puberty were recorded from captive specimens, and wild individuals experiencing variable food availability or lower mean temperatures might exhibit considerably delayed maturation schedules.

A particularly striking aspect of the reproductive biology of Gambusia puncticulata is its capacity for rapid population growth under favorable conditions. In laboratory populations held at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], the maximum recorded reproductive rate is achieved by combining a high fecundity per event with a frequent breeding schedule. Females produce litters of 30 young per spawning event [N_R_i = 30 young per spawning event] and are capable of producing up to 6 litters per year [F_R_i = up to 6 litters per year]. This combination of a moderately large brood size and high reproductive frequency is relatively unusual among poeciliids of similar body size, most of which produce smaller, more frequent litters or larger, less frequent ones. The rapid generational turnover facilitated by this high reproductive output makes the species a successful colonizer of disturbed habitats and intermittent water bodies throughout its Caribbean range.

The maximum recorded lifespan for Gambusia puncticulata was observed under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C], where the oldest individuals survived for 2.5 years [am = 2.5 years]. This is a modest longevity compared to many other members of the Cyprinodontiformes, likely reflecting the species' relatively high metabolic rate and the energetic costs associated with its elevated reproductive output. Field studies in seasonal ponds, however, suggest that wild lifespans are often considerably shorter due to predation pressure, desiccation events, and fluctuating food resources. When the rate of senescence is considered alongside the rapid attainment of puberty and the high frequency of reproduction, the demographic strategy of this species clearly prioritizes early and prolific breeding over the maintenance of somatic tissues into an extended old age.
